critic_text:
I did not recommend C. I rejected C-stated and recommended D: B’s terminal-window recovery, with reject as a **backstop**, not as the parse. Kimi’s counter lands on C-stated. It does not land on that.

**C-stated — withdraw.** The contract already requires the block directly above the verdict. An intervening fence is already a violation. A rule in force cannot be the remedy for its own violation. Agreed.

**C-enforced as “reject the reply” — exists, and is not silent drop.** Different objects:

- Silent drop: extraction fails, **admission succeeds**. Findings `[]`, verdict recorded, seat counts, debate looks complete. That is the completeness lie — fail-open admission.
- Reject: extraction fails, **admission fails**. No verdict written, seat does not count, debate is incomplete. Downstream must retry or HOLD. That is an honest zero.

Both leave the fenced bytes unread. Only silent drop counterfeits a critic. Reject refuses to. That distinction is why reject is not “the same bug.” Abandoning the admission gate because “you still didn’t read the findings” would keep the lie.

**C-enforced as the sole resolution — hold the rejection.** Reject-without-unfence is a halt, not a parse. It still throws away a record-shaped terminal window that is sitting in view. Retry re-asks a model that already wrapped; sticky wrappers loop; a retry cap then **under-invokes** a critic who already answered. Visible incompleteness is better than a counterfeit seat, but it is still information loss the parser can avoid. Enforcement that never reads the block is not a fix for wrapping — it is C with a red flag.

So: there is an enforced C (parse failure / incomplete debate). It differs from silent drop on **whether the verdict is admitted**. That difference does not make C the remedy. Recovery is still B, scoped to the terminal window (fence-only candidate ⇒ unfence; unfenced records above ⇒ fence is quote). Reject stays the gate for what B will not recover — empty window after discard, mixed residue, non-record-shaped fence — so ambiguity cannot count as a critic.

I hold D. I withdraw C, stated or enforced-as-sufficient. I hold that reject ≠ silent drop.

Severity: high
Mechanism: Taking “reject the reply” as the fix leaves the parser unchanged, so a fence-only terminal block is still not read. Retry depends on the same contract already violated; a cap drops the seat (`under_invoked`) even though the findings were in the fence.
Failure mode: Sticky wrapper loops, then a missing critic. Debate HALTs or proceeds short a seat. Recoverable majors/blockers stay unread — visible, but the same extraction miss.
Detection signal: Fenced record block + `verdict: concerns`, no unfenced records. Enforced-C-only yields parse failure/retry, never ingested findings. After cap, panel size < `critic_panel` with the wrapped text still in the raw reply.
Falsifier: Constrained decoding or an equivalent that makes an intervening fence unproducible, so reject never fires on wrap. Not contract prose.
Recommendation: Do not ship C. Unfence the fence-only terminal window (B); reject only what that rule does not recover.

Severity: medium
Mechanism: Collapsing reject into silent drop because both unread the fence erases the admission bit. That argument pushes either toward keeping counted `no_records` or toward A (ingest every fence).
Failure mode: Admission gate dropped; `concerns` with empty findings still records; completeness lie returns.
Detection signal: A design note that treats `IncompleteDebateError` as “the same as `no_records`.” Probe: reject path must not write a verdict; silent-drop path does.
Falsifier: Evidence the current parser already refuses to record a verdict on `no_records`. The incident description says it records one.
Recommendation: Keep the gate. Do not equate unread-and-counted with unread-and-refused.

- severity: major — reject-only C still does not read a fence-only terminal block; retry-cap under-invokes a critic who already answered
- severity: minor — reject is not silent drop: the seat must not count; collapsing them would drop the admission gate
verdict: concerns

Adopt the distinct parse state, but make it a **verdict gate**: zero findings, mark unread candidates, and withhold the critic’s verdict until retry or explicit escalation. If the verdict is still recorded normally, the blocker is only relocated; if it is withheld, the ambiguity becomes actionable rather than silent.

Severity: high  
Mechanism: A parse state without dispatch gating still permits an unsupported verdict to count, preserving the original evidence/verdict inconsistency.  
Failure mode: The system labels the seat as ambiguous but records `pass` or `concerns` as usable evidence.  
Detection signal: A fenced terminal block produces both an ambiguity marker and a committed verdict without retry/escalation.  
Falsifier: A dispatch invariant proving ambiguous parses cannot contribute a verdict to the aggregate.  
Recommendation: Hold until the ambiguity state suppresses verdict credit and triggers retry or explicit operator escalation.  
- severity: major — Ambiguity must block verdict credit, not merely annotate a zero-finding parse
verdict: concerns

**Hold.** The fourth state is the right parse-level design — it is what I argued for — and it is sufficient *if and only if* "visible to the caller" is pinned to mean "the caller cannot proceed." Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is where this fix would go to die.

**Why the state itself is correct.** It resolves the dilemma the two pinned cases created without touching either semantic: fenced-example stays ignored, fenced-findings stays ignored, and neither is *silently* ignored. It counts nothing, so it cannot inflate; it records nothing, so it cannot convert a `concerns` into an effective pass through the no_records path. It also has a clean detection rule, because the contract already contains the unambiguous encoding: a critic that wants to quote an example can fence the example and then put real records — or `findings: none` — *outside* the fence, directly above the verdict. So the fourth state fires exactly when the terminal region is neither clean records nor explicit `findings: none`. That is a precise definition of malformed, not a heuristic.

**Why "visible" alone is not sufficient.** A parse state is inert. Its disposition is decided by the caller, and an unspecified caller will do what unspecified callers always do with a new warning class: log it and continue, because the dispatch has a job to finish. That is the crying-wolf decay path in miniature — the drop becomes *documented* rather than *silent*, which feels like progress and changes nothing about what ships. The fourth state is sufficient only under three caller-side conditions, all of which need to be pinned in code, not described in a comment:

1. **Un-recordable.** When the state fires, no verdict is recorded — not a provisional one, not the literal token with a flag. The dispatch outcome is "unresolved," which blocks the same way a blocking verdict would.
2. **Bounded recovery.** Retry N times (small N — the same model with the same habits will often misfence identically), then escalate to the operator, with the raw reply attached either way.
3. **Audited.** The malformed event itself — reply, reason, dispatch ID — goes on the audit record. If only the parse layer knows, the sin has been moved up one level, exactly the failure I flagged originally.

**On the second question: does anything short of counting them let a real finding disappear?** Yes — within that dispatch, unavoidably. The fourth state does not recover the findings; it converts *silent, permanent* loss into *announced, deferred* loss. If the retry succeeds, the findings arrive and nothing was lost. If the bound fires, the finding is still uncounted, but the gate is now held by a human reading the raw reply — which is the correct end state for a one-shot machine read that failed. That residual is real and should be accepted explicitly rather than argued away: the alternative (counting through the fence) recovers the information in the good case and corrupts the verdict in the bad case, and you cannot tell which case you are in. Deferred-and-held beats counted-and-wrong.

One honest cost to keep on the record: the fourth state will produce false positives — a reply whose only fenced block is a genuine example, with nothing above it, trips malformed even though nothing was lost. That is the acceptable direction of error (it costs a retry or an operator glance), but it means C, the contract clause, remains load-bearing: every compliance improvement shrinks the malformed rate, and the malformed rate is now *measurable*, which it never was while the drop was silent.

So: hold the blocker. The fourth state is sufficient as the parse half of the fix; it is not yet a fix until the three caller conditions are pinned. Propose it as "add a state the caller will see" and I would block it; propose it as "add a state the caller cannot proceed past" and it clears.

verdict: concerns
